opening.headline: It deals with how to control the amount of thinking so that you can think sufficiently about difficult problems and answer simple problems without wasting time.
body: When solving difficult multi-step planning problems, models need to think things through. But more thinking slows down responses and increases costs. Spending too much time thinking about even simple classification tasks is a waste.

In this class, we will sequentially look at what inference tokens the inference model uses internally and how they are calculated, what the three companies call the settings that control the amount of thinking, and which instructions are correct for the inference model and which instructions should be omitted. At the end, we apply the settings to a simple classification task and a multi-step planning task to explain the rationale for our choices.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the meaning of inference model and inference strength settings
You can distinguish the strength of reasoning that matches the difficulty of the task.
Instruction methods that do not fit the inference model can be identified.
By writing down the intermediate steps, you can explain the principles of increasing accuracy and the process by which the inference model acquires them.

screens.title: I want to think about it for a long time, but I'm worried about the cost.
screens.lead: When we increase the amount of thinking, we first look at what we gain and what we pay. Read the scene below and think about the two-way relationship.

visual.alt: A scene showing a difficult planning problem on the left and the quality, speed, and cost dashboards on the right.
labels: Relocation plan that satisfies the schedule and budget constraints of all three departments

paragraphs: Let's say you need to plan an office relocation that meets the schedule and budget constraints of three departments. Constraints are intertwined, so shifting one department's schedule can shake up another department's budget. These multi-level planning problems can only be solved if the model has been thought through.

However, increasing your thinking comes with a price. The more steps the model goes through internally, the slower it responds, and the more tokens it costs to think about it. Conversely, if you spend too much time thinking about simple classification of customer inquiries into 'delivery', 'refund', and 'other', you will not gain anything even if you spend the same amount of money.

The question for this class is this. How do you balance the amount of thought you put into each task? The answer lies in knowing where thoughts arise, what they control, and how much is needed for which tasks.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: As you increase your thinking, speed and cost decrease as much as quality increases. What would be the benefit of being able to set this trade-off differently for each task?

screens.outro: Now that we have established the trade-off, let us recall your experience.

screens.title: Recall the moment when AI was ‘thinking’
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You will not enter or submit your answer, so think for yourself first and then click.

items.prompt: Have you ever had a ‘thinking’ sign appear for a long time before coming up with an answer?
items.answer: That sign is the time the inference model spends thinking internally before coming up with an answer. Although it is not visible to the eye, the token is being used during that time. In this lesson we will see how those tokens are calculated.

items.prompt: Has there ever been a time when you had the same question, but sometimes you got an immediate answer and sometimes it took a long time?
items.answer: Claude documents that thinking is adaptive. Because the model determines whether and how much to think for each request, it may answer simple questions right away and think for a long time about complex questions. Even the same question can vary depending on the situation.

items.prompt: Was the prompt ‘Think about it step by step’ really necessary?
items.answer: OpenAI advises that phrases that are helpful in a general model may be unnecessary or even a hindrance in an inference model. This is because you are asking the model that already thinks step by step internally to do it again. Find out why in the following screen.

screens.outro: Let me start by explaining where thoughts arise.

screens.title: Inference Token: The Invisible Cost of Thought
screens.lead: Select the arrows to step through the steps and see where thoughts are placed and how they are calculated as requests turn into responses.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the response structure and billing range, with a question followed by a thinking block and a text block.
labels: Counted as output tokens, included in max_tokens

steps.title: A question comes in
steps.body: When a user sends a question, the model may not start writing an answer right away. The inference model goes through an internal thinking phase before coming up with an answer. The OpenAI documentation explains that the inference model uses an internal inference token before generating a response, which allows it to make plans, explore alternatives, and solve difficult multi-step problems.

steps.title: Thoughts come out as thinking blocks
steps.body: In Claude's response, this thought may come as a thinking block at the front of the response. The Gemini article also explains that the thinking stage appears in the response. However, the summary may be empty, depending on the settings or if the model did not infer sufficiently.

steps.title: The answer continues in a text block
steps.body: After the thought is finished, a text block follows with the answer to be shown to the user. This is usually what users read. The entire response is made up of thought blocks and answer blocks, and costs are incurred in both, even if only the answer is visible to the user.

steps.title: Thoughts are also counted as output tokens
steps.body: The Claude documentation explains that tokens written to thoughts are charged as output tokens, even if no thought text is returned. This token is also included with the answer in `max_tokens`. So, if your thoughts get longer, the space available for your answer may decrease.

steps.title: The thoughts you see are not the original text.
steps.body:
The thought text you see on the screen may be a summary rather than the original text. The Claude document reveals that the text in the thinking block is a summary of the model's reasoning and not the original thought process. Just because the summary is short does not mean the idea is short, so usage should be checked by aggregated tokens rather than visible characters.

There is no guarantee that the thoughts shown, whether summarized or original text, are an exact record of the model's actual judgment process. One study reported that embedding a cue in the input that tilted the answer to one side changed the model's answer, but the cue was barely mentioned in the step-by-step instructions. In Anthropic's inference model experiments, there were many cases where the model used clues but did not reveal them in its thinking process. So read the thought text as a clue to where to suspect, but not as evidence for your judgment.

screens.outro: Now that we know that thoughts cost money, let's look at settings that control the amount of thoughts.

ext.title: Turpin et al., Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
Anthropic, Reasoning models don't always say what they think

screens.title: Why Thinking Becomes Accurate: Middle Tokens Are Calculation
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how accuracy increases when the model writes intermediate steps and how the inference model goes through this process.

tabs.label: One token calculation
tabs.body:
To understand the concept, simply put, the model goes through one calculation of a given size when creating one token. Even if the answer is one word or one number, all judgment must be completed within that one calculation.

For questions that involve one or two steps, this calculation is sufficient. However, if you ask students to immediately answer a question that involves multiple steps, the risk of making a mistake increases because they have to draw a conclusion first without being able to write down intermediate results anywhere.

tabs.label: Solving intermediate steps in writing
tabs.body:
When the intermediate steps are written, calculations are added once for each token written, and the result of the previous step is input to the next calculation. This method of unraveling steps and reaching an answer is called a chain of thought.

For example, if you ask them to answer straight away, ‘What if I buy three items worth 12,000 won, pay 3,000 won for shipping, and then take 10 percent off the total?’, it is easy to skip the intermediate price. On the other hand, if you write steps like '36,000 won in total, 39,000 won including shipping cost, 35,100 won after 10 percent discount,' each step becomes the basis for the next step. A study by Wei et al. reported that prompting with examples illustrating intermediate stages of reasoning increased performance on arithmetic, general knowledge, and symbolic reasoning tasks, and that this effect was evident in sufficiently large models.

tabs.label: How are inference models created?
tabs.body:
An inference model is a model trained so that this process occurs without the user having to do it every time. In the introduction to o1, OpenAI explains that it trained this model using reinforcement learning to create a long chain of internal thoughts before answering, and that through training, it noticed and corrected mistakes, divided difficult steps into easy steps, and tried a different approach when it got stuck.

The DeepSeek-R1 paper also reports that behaviors such as self-examination, verification, and strategy change occurred using reinforcement learning alone without human-written reasoning examples, and that performance increased in tasks such as math and coding where the correct answer can be automatically confirmed. This exercise allows the thought to be used as an internal token at the beginning of the response.

tabs.label: How much thought should I use?
tabs.body:
More thinking doesn't always mean things get better. A study by Snell et al. reported that it was more efficient to divide the amount of calculations used at the time of inference according to the difficulty of the problem, and that in some problems, small models used additional calculations and outperformed much larger models.

This principle explains two things. First, it is right to lower the intensity of reasoning because a lot of thinking is wasted on easy problems. Second, telling a reasoning model that already thinks step-by-step internally to think step-by-step may be redundant and therefore unnecessary or intrusive.

screens.outro: Now that you know the principles, let's compare the settings that actually control the amount of thoughts you have.

ext.title: Wei et al., Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

data.notes: All three companies follow the same principles. Lower intensity is advantageous for speed and cost, while higher intensity is advantageous for complex problems. In Claude's documentation, low is described as the most efficient level for simple, fast tasks like subagents. In adaptive thinking, simple factual questions may not have a thinking block at all, so you should not assume that every response has a thought. If you want to make yourself think less, the document recommends lowering the intensity first before trying to block it with a prompt. The setting names and value ranges vary by model, so you should check the documentation for the model you want to use to see what values ​​are supported. As shown in the last row of the table, the terminology for the way of thinking itself varies from company to company, so do not assume that they are the same function just by looking at the name, but compare based on whether the roles are the same.

screens.outro: Now that we know the setup, let's move on to the instruction method that fits our inference model.

screens.title: Instructions for inference models: what to leave out
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the prompts change when you assign the same task to a regular model and an inference model.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing the long prompts for the generic model on the left with the concise prompts for the inference model on the right.
labels: Write down your entire thought process.

states.label: For regular models
states.body:
Since a general model produces an answer immediately, the results may be improved if the intermediate process is written down. So sentences like this are often included in the prompt.

```
You are a relocation planning expert.
Think about it step by step.
Write down your entire thought process and write a conclusion at the end.
The budget must be less than 50 million won.
```

The second and third lines of this prompt are sentences that ask the model to think for you. For models who do not think internally, this sentence becomes a thought-getting tool.

states.label: For inference model
states.body:
OpenAI tells us that inference models work best with simple, direct prompts. Instructions such as ‘think step by step’ may be unhelpful or hindering to models that already internally think step by step.

```
Goal: Create a plan to relocate three departments within two months
Success Criteria: Satisfy schedule constraints for all departments
Constraints: Total budget less than 50 million won
<input>
(Departmental schedule and budget table)
</input>
```

These instructions recommend dividing your input with delimiters, trying without examples at first, and adding examples only when necessary. It is a good idea to specifically write down the success criteria and constraints of the target outcome.

Claude's documentation also explains that when Thinking is on, prompts to write down your thought process may be rejected and that it is better to leave that to the Thinking function. Additionally, OpenAI introduces a common configuration in which planning and judgment are handled by an inference model, and repetitive execution is handled by a fast GPT model.

screens.outro: Now that we have organized the instruction method, let's look at what tasks the inference model is suitable for.

screens.title: When is the inference model right: planners and executors?
screens.lead: Choosing a task type will reveal whether you're a planner or executor and why. Decide for yourself which one you want first and then press it.

visual.alt: A flowchart in which the inferential model handles planning and judgment, and the fast model executes the steps.
labels: Accuracy and trust first → Planner / Speed and cost first → Executor

items.prompt: Tasks that require vague requests and understanding of intent
items.answer: The planner (inference model) is correct. OpenAI Guidance explains that the inference model is strong at understanding user intent from limited or scattered information and handling gaps in instructions. It is said that when there is insufficient information, people often ask questions before making a guess.

items.prompt: The task of finding only the key points from a large amount of data
items.answer: The planner is right. Inference models are useful for making decisions based on large amounts of ambiguous information. The longer and more disjointed the material, the greater the benefit of thinking.

items.prompt: The task of creating a multi-step plan that satisfies multiple constraints
items.answer: The planner is right. Problems where there are dependencies between steps and overlapping constraints are suitable for inference models to develop strategies. After creating this plan, the task of executing each step can be handed over to a quick model.

The planner is right. Code review involves looking at multiple parts together and determining where mistakes are made, so inference models are very useful. OpenAI guidance is a representative use case for inference models.

items.prompt: Iterative task of classifying formatted inquiries
items.answer: The executor (GPT model) is correct. If the tasks are clearly defined and speed and cost are priorities, the fast GPT model makes more sense. If you think about this for a long time, the cost will only increase.

items.prompt: The plan is already out and the work is done to execute each step in bulk.
items.answer: The executor is correct. OpenAI explains that within a workflow, it is common to have a combination of an inferential model making plans and decisions and a fast model executing the steps. For most inference tasks, we recommend starting with a base model and considering smaller models if cost and delay are important.

screens.outro: Now that we have seen the criteria for judging types of work, let's apply them to two cases.

screens.title: Case Commentary 1: A simple classification task
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of choosing settings for a simple classification task. Select the arrows to follow the instructions from the difficulty assessment.

steps.title: work
steps.body: This task classifies customer inquiries into ‘Delivery’, ‘Refund’, or ‘Other’. Thousands of messages come in every day, and each one is a short sentence.

steps.title: Difficulty judgment
steps.body: Classification rules are clear. The judgment is made in one step, and the same thing is repeated in large numbers. It is not a problem of satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously or having dependencies between steps. Therefore, the benefits of deep thinking are small.

steps.title: Select settings
steps.body: Choose a low inference strength. Claude considers low, Gemini considers minimal or low, and OpenAI considers low or lower as candidates. If your model supports a lightweight model, you can also use the lightweight model. Common simple tasks are the job of the executor, not the planner.

steps.title: basis
steps.body: The Claude article describes low as the most efficient level for simple tasks where speed and low cost are most important, such as subagents. OpenAI also advises that at low intensity, the response is faster and there are fewer tokens. The larger the number, the greater the benefit of reducing thought tokens.

steps.title: directive
steps.body:
Just write down the classification criteria and output format concisely.

```
Categorize customer inquiries into delivery, refund, or other.
Please write only one word of the category name in your answer.
<inquiry>
(Original text of customer inquiry)
</inquiry>
```

Do not include sentences that say ‘explain your thought process’. This is because it only increases unnecessary thought tokens. There is no need to worry about shortened instructions. If the classification criteria and output format are clear, the model will provide consistent answers.

screens.outro: Now that you've solved the easy side, let's move on to the other side: pyramid schemes.

screens.title: Case Commentary 2: Developing a multi-step plan
screens.lead: Your instructor will guide you through the difficult planning tasks of choosing a setting and managing costs. Select the arrows and follow them step by step.

steps.title: work
steps.body: The task is to create an office relocation plan that satisfies the schedule and budget constraints of all three departments. You only have to do it once, and the results determine the quality of your entire plan.

steps.title: Difficulty judgment
steps.body: Constraints overlap and the dependencies between steps are large. Changing one department's move date changes the budgets and schedules of other departments as well. These matters are the job of the planner and should be given plenty of thought.

steps.title: Select settings
steps.body: Pick a top model with high intensity (high or higher) and adaptive thinking turned on. In Claude, you start with a high model, and for more difficult tasks you can increase it to xhigh or max. Since this is a one-time operation, there is good reason to accept the increased cost.

steps.title: cost management
steps.body: You can also find it by reducing it instead of setting it at the highest level from the beginning. The document recommends that you reduce the intensity in steps of the same input, finding the lightest setting that meets your quality criteria. This exploration is most effective when the same task is repeated.

steps.title: directive
steps.body:
Be specific about your goals, success criteria, and constraints, and divide your input into separators.

```
Goal: Create a plan to relocate three departments within two months
Success Criteria: Satisfy schedule constraints for all departments and have no disruption to work.
Constraints: Total budget less than 50 million won
<departments>
(Departmental schedule and budget table)
</departments>
```

I do not include sentences asking you to think step by step. The model does the thinking.

steps.title: Compare the two cases
steps.body: Classification is low-intensity with lightweight models and concise instructions, while planning is high-intensity with high-level models and specific standards and constraints. The point in both cases is that the instructions do not require step-by-step thinking. What changes is the setting that determines the amount of thinking.

screens.outro: Now that we've completed the two cases, let's summarize the main points.

screens.title: Standards for matching the amount of thought to the task
screens.lead: Let's organize the concepts covered in this class by connecting them to the first question.

paragraphs: The first question was how to balance the amount of thinking for each task. You now have three tools: First, inference tokens are tokens that the model uses for internal thinking, and are counted as output tokens even if they are not visible on the screen. Next, the inference strength is the knob that adjusts the amount of these tokens, and all three companies offer levels from low to high. Finally, adaptive thinking lets the model decide whether and how much to think for each request.

The order of adjustment is as follows. If the task is simple and repetitive, use low intensity and concise instructions. If it is a difficult task with overlapping constraints, use high intensity and specific success criteria. When you want to reduce your thoughts, lower the intensity first before blocking them with a prompt.

Inference models do not include instructions to think step-by-step. Instead, clearly write down your goals, success criteria, and constraints and divide your input into separators. Remember, the goal is to find the lightest setup that meets your quality standards.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: Increasing the intensity is not necessarily better, but the lightest setting that meets the quality required by the work is a good choice.

checks.q: What is the most appropriate reason why a model becomes more accurate when answering a calculation problem that requires multiple steps by writing down the intermediate steps?
options: This is because calculations are added to each unwritten token, and the result of the previous step becomes the material for the next calculation.
This is because while solving the problem, the model searches for the correct answer on the Internet.
This is because as the article becomes longer, the knowledge cutoff is pushed back.
This is because using an intermediate step turns off stochastic generation.
checks.explain: If you write out the intermediate steps, calculations are added for each token, and the intermediate results become the input for the next step. An inference model is a model that has been trained through this process.

wrong.1: Writing intermediate steps and searching are separate things, and searching only happens when you turn on the tool.
wrong.2: The knowledge cutoff is when learning is completed, so it does not change with the length of the article.
wrong.3: Even if the intermediate steps are solved, the method of probabilistically selecting the next token remains the same.

checks.q: I asked Claude a simple question and he got the answer right away, without any thinking blocks. What is the best explanation?
options: Claude's thinking is adaptive, so the model decides whether and how much to think for each request, and may not think for simple questions.
If you do not see the thought text, it always means that the inference token has not been charged.
If effort is high, every request must have a thinking block attached.
The prompt didn’t say ‘Think step by step’ so I lost my mind.
checks.explain: Adaptive thinking allows the model to determine whether and how much thinking is needed for each request, so simple questions may not have thinking blocks.

wrong.1: This must be distinguished from the fact that Thought Tokens may be charged even if only the summary is visible or hidden.
wrong.2: Effort affects overall token usage as well as thoughts, but does not enforce the presence or absence of a block.
wrong.3: Whether or not a thought occurs depends on the model's adaptive judgment and intensity settings, not on its directive sentence.

checks.q: We're looking to improve the prompts we send to our inference model. What is the most appropriate direction?

Instead of thinking, provide instructions to write down the thought process.

glossary.def: This is a token that the model uses to think internally before coming up with an answer. Counted as output token.
Settings that control how much the model spends on thinking and output. The lower the faster and cheaper, the higher the more thought out.
This method allows the model to decide whether and how much to think based on the complexity of the request.
This is a setting that specifies the level of thinking in Gemini from minimal to high.
It is a method of reasoning by writing down the intermediate steps leading to the answer. The inference model is equipped with this process internally as training.

misconceptions.myth: Asking people to ‘think about it step by step’ always results in better results.
misconceptions.fact: While this may be helpful in a general model, it may be unnecessary or disruptive to the inference model we already think about internally.

misconceptions.myth: If you don't see the thought text, you're not thinking.
misconceptions.fact: Thought tokens are counted as output tokens, even if only the summary is visible or hidden. Usage is determined by aggregated tokens, not visible letters.

misconceptions.myth: The higher the inference strength, the better.
misconceptions.fact: It's a waste for simple tasks. The goal is to find the lightest setup that meets quality standards.

misconceptions.myth: By reading the thinking text, you can see exactly how the model made its decisions.
misconceptions.fact: There is no guarantee that the thoughts or explanations shown are a direct record of the actual judgment process. Read only the clues that tell you where to suspect, and check separately if they are right or wrong.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Inference tokens are used for internal thinking and are counted as output tokens.
Inference strength is the lever that trades off speed, cost, and quality.
Adaptive thinking lets the model determine the amount of thinking per request.
Reasoning models require concise, specific instructions and do not require step-by-step thinking instructions.

Solving the intermediate steps in writing increases the accuracy by adding calculations, and the inference model is equipped with this as training, but there is no guarantee that the visible thoughts are a record of the actual judgment.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Among the tasks I often entrust to AI, which do I want to make it think about for a long time and which do I want to finish quickly?
